# R5 Digest — Reign of Saul 13–15 (8141–10111)
**Source:** Tsumura, *The First Book of Samuel* (NICOT, 2006), commentary on 1 Sam 13:1–15:35  
**Reader:** extraction subagent R5  
**Coverage:** slice `R5_saul_reign_8141-10111.txt` read in full (slice L1–1971 = raw **8141–10111**); section C “Reign of Saul (13:1–15:35)” through end of ch. 15 (before ch. 16).

## Claims

### C-R5-01 | Literary frame: rejection of Saul, build-up to David
- **Claim (Tsumura):** After Samuel’s address (ch. 12), chs. 13–15 move quickly toward Saul’s rejection; 13:1 may emphasize the shortness of Saul’s reign “in God’s eyes.” Chs. 13–15 build toward choosing David, Saul’s “neighbor” (15:28), as God’s anointed. Literarily Saul’s rejection and David’s rise form a **&lt;not A but B&gt;** pattern. Gordon: “the dominant feeling in chs. 13–15 is not of success, but of failure.” Saul is twice rejected for disregard of God’s word (13:13; 15:11, 23), against Samuel’s warning not to act wickedly (12:25).
- **Quote:** “the following three chapters, chs. 13–15, are therefore a build-up toward the climax of choosing David, Saul’s neighbor (15:28), as God’s anointed. From a literary perspective, Saul’s rejection and David’s rise thus constitute a &lt;not A but B&gt; pattern.”
- **Locus:** §C intro / p. 330 / slice ~L1–6
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-02 | 13:1 summary: MT “two years” as ironic divine valuation
- **Claim:** 13:1 is incomplete accession formula; age missing; MT preserves “two” for length of reign though actual reign was almost certainly longer (Acts 13:21 / Josephus forty years; Josephus elsewhere twenty). Tsumura rejects easy restoration of numerals (NIV thirty/forty-two; NASB forty/thirty-two, etc.). Preferred literary reading: **ironic** — *ben-šānāh* may mean a certain age; “just for two years” is from the author’s/God’s point of view: after ch. 13 Saul is no longer “king” in God’s sight (v. 14). “Two” is the smallest cardinal in series; expression for a very short time.
- **Quote:** “the expression just for two years is probably given from the author’s, hence God’s, point of view: Saul was king only for ‘two years,’ even though he remained ‘king’ much longer in human eyes; after ch. 13, Saul is no longer ‘king’ in God’s sight (see v. 14).”
- **Locus:** 13:1 / pp. 331–333 / slice ~L10–36
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[saul]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R5-03 | Standing army; Jonathan introduced; Michmash / Geba geography
- **Claim:** Saul chooses 3,000 standing troops (2,000 with him at Michmash “in the mountain of Bethel”; 1,000 with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin). *Thousand* may be unit or actual number. Pre-monarchy militia vs Saul’s standing cadre (cf. 14:52). Jonathan first appears without explanation; name “Yah[weh] has given” implies Saul’s family worshipped Yahweh. Jonathan strikes Philistine *neṣîb* (singular: prefect/governor, not “garrison”) at Geba — effective military blow initiating long war.
- **Quote:** “Saul’s establishment of a cadre of three thousand men provides Israel with a standing army (cf. 14:52).” / “The singular noun neṣîb … probably refers to a person, either prefect … or ‘governor’ … not ‘garrison.’”
- **Locus:** 13:2–3a / pp. 334–336 / slice ~L37–66
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[jonathan]], [[philistines]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R5-04 | Philistine mobilization; Israelites hide; Gilgal muster
- **Claim:** After Jonathan’s strike, Philistines hear Saul’s horn-blast “Let the Hebrews hear!” (AXB / literary insertion; not necessarily “Hebrews have revolted” as LXX). All Israel hears that “Saul struck” (credit to king for subordinate’s act, ANE parallel). Philistines muster huge force (30,000 chariotry MT / or units; 6,000 cavalry; people like sand) at Michmash east of Beth-awen; Israelites hide in caves/holes; some Hebrews flee Transjordan (Gad/Gilead). Saul at Gilgal (strategic + cultic; link to 10:8 / 11:15).
- **Quote:** “Saul’s summoning the people to Gilgal, the ancient cultic center, must have had a strategic (military) purpose … as well as a religious purpose.”
- **Locus:** 13:3b–7a / pp. 336–340 / slice ~L67–130
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[philistines]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R5-05 | First rejection scene: waiting seven days; sacrifice; not mere 10:8 continuation
- **Claim:** Saul waits seven days for *mô‘ēd* — not necessarily “time set by Samuel” but **appointed feast** on cultic calendar when Samuel would be at Gilgal (annual circuit 7:16). “Waiting” is consecration / waiting on God before battle, not only waiting for Samuel’s person — so 10:8 and 13:8 need not be the same occasion though both at Gilgal. Saul offers burnt offering (not yet peace offerings) when Samuel fails to appear and troops scatter. Discourse structure (SETTING/EVENT) supports reading 13 as literary whole; against redactional isolation of 7b–15a.
- **Quote:** “it is likely that everybody knew when Samuel was supposed to be in Gilgal… the text has nothing to do with a personal appointment Samuel made with Saul.” / “These features rather support reading the entire section of ch. 13 as a literary whole.”
- **Locus:** 13:7b–9; discourse analysis / pp. 340–344 / slice ~L132–420
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R5-06 | Saul’s excuses: sight not faith; contrast with Jonathan
- **Claim:** Saul’s excuses (troops scatter; Samuel late; Philistines gathering; favor of Lord not entreated) “seem totally legitimate” but he judges by what he **saw**, not by faith. Sharp contrast with Jonathan in ch. 14 (numbers irrelevant if Lord acts). What Saul should wait for: Samuel’s intercession and instruction (12:23), not mere physical presence.
- **Quote:** “Saul judged the situation according to what he saw, not by faith in the Lord. Note the sharp contrast between Saul here and Jonathan in ch. 14.”
- **Locus:** 13:10–12 / pp. 345–346 / slice ~L425–481
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[jonathan]], [[samuel]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R5-07 | First rejection (13:13–14): dynasty will not continue; “man of his choice”
- **Claim:** Samuel: “You have acted foolishly! … You have not kept the commandment of the Lord… For now, the Lord would have established your kingdom over Israel **forever**! But now, **your kingdom will not endure**! The Lord has sought out for himself a **man of his choice**… and commanded him as **prince** (*nāgîd*) over his people.” *mamlaktekā lō’-tāqûm* = Saul cannot establish a dynasty (son will not succeed); 15:23 will reject Saul himself. *biqqēš* prophetic perfect; “man according to his heart” = David (named “neighbor” only at 15:28). *kwn* “established” foreshadows 2 Sam 7 dynastic language. “Eternal kingdom” idea not foreign even early monarchy. After indictment Saul musters only ~600 (20% of original 3,000).
- **Quote:** “The expression your kingdom will not endure … suggests that Saul cannot establish a dynasty, let alone an eternal dynasty … — his son will not succeed him. In addition, in 15:23 Saul himself will be rejected from being king.” / “The phrase a man of his choice (lit., ‘a man according to his heart’) refers to David.”
- **Locus:** 13:13–15 / pp. 346–349 / slice ~L452–516
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R5-08 | Nature of Saul’s “commandment” offense (13) — not priestly usurpation primary
- **Claim:** No specific commandment named in ch. 13. Hypotheses: (1) usurping prophet’s holy-war role / not seeking oracle through Samuel; (2) dual king-priest role — Gordon rejects pure priestly usurpation (14:33–35; David/Solomon sacrifices). Tsumura: 10:8 “wait seven days” unlikely (years earlier; Saul kept it and was made king 11:15). Prefer: commandment concerns **nature/status of king** — carry out God’s word as people’s representative especially for holy war; listen to prophet’s word. Foolishness may be failure to acknowledge prophet’s higher role, not merely the sacrifice. “Rejecting the word of the Lord” is thread into total rejection (15:11, 13, 19, 22, 23).
- **Quote:** “the ‘foolishness’ of Saul might possibly be not so much in his sacrificing the burnt offering as his failure to acknowledge the prophet’s higher role as the divine messenger and to listen to the word of God.”
- **Locus:** 13:13 comment / pp. 346–348 / slice ~L494–507
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R5-09 | Philistine raiders; metalworker monopoly; garrison as ch. 14 link
- **Claim:** Philistine *hammašḥît* raiders in three divisions (Ophrah/Shual; Beth-horon; border/Zeboim). **Embedded discourse 13:19–22:** no metal worker in Israel; Philistines prevent Hebrews making swords/spears; Israelites go down to sharpen agricultural tools; price *paim* (two-thirds shekel); on day of war only Saul and Jonathan have swords/spears — magnifies Lord’s victory via Jonathan. *maṣṣab* “garrison” at Michmash Pass is key-word link (Ab/B) into ch. 14.
- **Quote:** “Now no metal worker was found in all the land of Israel, for the Philistines thought that the Hebrews should not make swords or spears.” / “The fact that the Israelites did not have ‘swords and spears’ suggests that any victory for them would come from the Lord.”
- **Locus:** 13:16–23 / pp. 349–353 / slice ~L517–630
- **Targets:** [[philistines]], [[jonathan]], [[saul]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R5-10 | Ch. 14 frame: Saul vs Jonathan; Jonathan transitional to David
- **Claim:** Ch. 14 “masterpiece of narrative storytelling.” Contrast: Saul obsesses over troop numbers (3,000→600); Jonathan only whether Lord will act — “no hindrance for the Lord to save, whether by many or by few” (14:6). Jonathan’s faith act **sandwiched** by Saul’s two disobediences (chs. 13 and 15). Only Saul and Jonathan armed (13:22) — victory not by armed might. Klein: Jonathan transitional figure to David (battle leadership; people’s affection 14:45). Partial fulfillment of 9:16 (save from Philistines).
- **Quote:** “It is impressive that this incident of Jonathan’s act of trust is sandwiched by two incidents of Saul’s acts of disobedience in chs. 13 and 15.”
- **Locus:** 14 intro / pp. 354–355 / slice ~L631–640
- **Targets:** [[jonathan]], [[saul]], [[1-samuel]], [[philistines]]

### C-R5-11 | Jonathan’s raid: sign, uncircumcised, God-caused panic
- **Claim:** On “that day” of garrison move (13:23), Jonathan and armor-bearer cross without informing Saul. Sign protocol: if Philistines say “Come up toward us!” Lord has given them into hand (perfect of confidence; name Jonathan = “the Lord has given”). *‘ālênû* = “toward us” not necessarily “against.” Philistines call them “Hebrews… out of the holes.” First strike ~20 men in half-yoke field area. *ḥerdat ’ĕlōhîm*: God-caused trembling; earth shook — not merely human panic. *nth byd* “give into hand” ANE-wide, not only Deuteronomistic.
- **Quote:** “Perhaps is not a sign of Jonathan’s doubt in God’s ability, but rather a confession that God is not required to act for them.” / “the reference to God suggests that the ‘trembling’ was not caused simply by Jonathan’s first attack but by the hand of God.”
- **Locus:** 14:1–15 / pp. 355–364 / slice ~L644–905
- **Targets:** [[jonathan]], [[philistines]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R5-12 | Saul interrupts oracle; ark + ephod; careless divine matters
- **Claim:** Saul orders Ahijah “Bring near the ark of God” (MT; some prefer ephod with LXX) then “Withdraw your hand!” as tumult grows. Tsumura keeps MT ark: ephod already worn (v. 3); Saul may inquire by ephod before ark; “withdraw hand” idiom elsewhere for ephod (23:9; 30:7). Ark could be brought temporarily from Kiriath-jearim “on that day.” Two commands show careless attitude toward divine object and method; Saul “prays when he should act and acts when he should pray.” Battle: Philistines kill each other (*mehûmāh*); Lord saves Israel that day (14:23). Hebrews (former Philistine-side) and hiders in Ephraim join pursuit.
- **Quote:** “Saul is a person who prays when he should act and acts when he should pray. Such inconsistency is one of Saul’s characteristics.”
- **Locus:** 14:16–23 / pp. 364–368 / slice ~L909–976
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[jonathan]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R5-13 | Saul’s rash oath; honey; “troubled the land”
- **Claim:** Already abandoned after 13:13–14, Saul’s subsequent acts fail to satisfy God though surface success remains. Oath: cursed be who eats before evening when Saul avenges enemies — “grandiose gesture of self-denial” to influence Yahweh (McCarter via Tsumura). Jonathan eats honey unknowingly; eyes brighten (physiological + assonance *‘arar*/*‘or* per Gordon). Jonathan: father “disturbed/troubled” (*‘ākar*) the country — ominous root (Achan; Elijah/Ahab). Troops later eat blood (Lev prohibition); Saul builds first altar, proper slaughter on large stone — first serious attempt to worship though already rejected as king in Lord’s sight.
- **Quote:** “To be religious was not enough in the sight of the Lord who sees inside the heart (see 16:7).” / “While Saul was stubbornly religious, Jonathan was, by contrast, practically God-fearing.”
- **Locus:** 14:24–35 / pp. 368–376 / slice ~L979–1136
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[jonathan]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R5-14 | Lot-casting; Urim/Thummim; brachylogy *happîlû*; people rescue Jonathan
- **Claim:** God silent when Saul inquires night pursuit (withholding = unfavorable). Lots like Achan/Saul election: *nilkad* “taken,” *yṣ’* “freed.” MT “Give *tamim*!” abbreviated (audience knew procedure); not necessarily long LXX haplography. Urim/Thummim possibly two colored stones; related to ANE psephomancy (Horowitz/Hurowitz). 14:42 *happîlû* without “lots” = **brachylogy** (ellipsis of *gôrāl*); still means “decide” — McCarter’s haplography misses linguistic style. People reverse Saul’s “as Lord lives” death oath with same formula; *pdh* “rescued” (metaphorical). Jonathan nearly destroyed as potential dynastic heir mid-victory.
- **Quote:** “Here it is a brachylogy, namely, an ellipsis of the understood noun ‘lots,’ and the verb happîlû by itself keeps the idiomatic meaning ‘decide’ (impv.).”
- **Locus:** 14:36–46 / pp. 376–382 / slice ~L1137–1288
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[jonathan]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R5-15 | 14:47–52 summary; Amalek link; recruitment; war “all days of Saul”
- **Claim:** Favorable summary: Saul fights Moab, Ammon, Edom, Zobah kings, Philistines, Amalek; acts valiantly, delivers Israel from plunderers. Amalek = archetypal plunderers (Exod 17 etc.); **Ab/B link** into ch. 15. Family list (Jonathan, Ishvi, Malchishua; Merab, Michal; Ahinoam; Abner son of Ner); genealogy reconstruction. 14:52: Philistine war severe all Saul’s days; recruits *’îš gibbôr* / *ben-ḥayil* for standing army. Human progress vs spiritual decline; without Samuel’s instruction (12:23) disobedience worsens toward ch. 15 final rejection.

### C-R5-16 | Ch. 15 pivot: two rejections not mere doublets; “Saul dead while he lives”
- **Claim:** Chs. 15–16 pivotal: 15 ends rise-of-monarchy account with Saul’s failure/rejection; 16 new beginning (David). Saul remains king among people but “rejected king” in God’s sight (hinted 13:1 “couple of years”). Gordon: “Saul is dead while he still lives.” Inclusio: chosen (10:24) → rejected; became king by people’s voice (8:9, 22; 12:1), rejected for listening to people’s voice (15:20, 24). Wellhausen tradition of 13:7b–15a // 15 as doublets (both Gilgal, obedience, prophetic judgment form) — Tsumura: clear difference (13: failure of **dynasty**; 15: rejection of **Saul as king** / spirit withdrawal) but same author progressive stages; both about disobedience to commandment. Do not over-separate the two issues.
- **Quote:** “In ch. 13, Saul was told he could not found a dynasty because of disobedience; here he even more directly disregards the word of the Lord, and the Lord rejects him as king.”
- **Locus:** 15 intro / pp. 386–388 / slice ~L1389–1408

### C-R5-17 | Ḥerem command: Amalek remembrance; utterly destroy; ANE *ḥrm*
- **Claim:** Samuel (kingmaker) commands Saul: listen to words of Lord. Lord of hosts has “taken note” (*pqd* // Deut 25:17 *zkr*) of Amalek’s attack on faint Israel at Rephidim (Exod 17:8–13; Deut 25:17–19 blot-out command). **15:3:** go and strike Amalek; *wehaḥăramtem … welō’ taḥmōl* (&lt;A-not B&gt;): utterly destroy / put under ban; no compassion; kill man/woman, child/infant, ox/sheep, camel/donkey. *ḥrm*: common Semitic “separate, sacred”; Moabite Mesha stele (Nebo ban); Ugaritic Anath; semantic range consecrate → utterly destroy enemy / booty. Bible: devote as Yahweh’s share; often all living killed (Josh 6:21); metals to treasury. Deut 20: distant cities spare people; in-land cities total *ḥerem* against syncretism; here ban based on Deut 25:19. Gordon: ban/holy war far from NT Christian code — “provisional morality of OT”; Christian analogue “spiritual warfare” (Eph 6:12). Livestock under ban here (not always). Principle applies only in theocracy; human politicians lack right to declare vengeance.
- **Quote:** “In the Bible, it denotes to devote or set aside something as Yahweh’s share or booty. Usually all living things — men, women, children, and livestock — were killed, as in this verse and Josh. 6:21.” / “the institution of the ‘ban,’ like the whole concept of the holy war, is far removed from the Christian code of the New Testament and must be seen in the context of the provisional morality of the Old Testament.”
- **Locus:** 15:1–3 / pp. 388–391 / slice ~L1410–1467
- **Targets:** [[herem]], [[herem-canaanite-conquest]], [[amalekites]], [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[1-samuel]]
- **Flag:** *ḥerem* — controversy / reception

### C-R5-18 | Saul spares Agag and best livestock — partial ban disobedience
- **Claim:** Saul musters at Telaim (200,000 foot + 10,000 Judah; large numbers possible years after ch. 14). Spares Kenites (ḥesed from Exodus era). Strikes Amalek Havilah to Shur. Captures **Agag** alive (name/title; Haman “Agagite” as type of Yahweh’s enemy); utterly destroys people with sword. **15:9:** Saul **and the people** spare Agag and best cattle/lambs/all good; destroy only despised/worthless. Direct disobedience to v. 3; purpose was not spoil but ancient command; “partial fulfillment is not a possibility” in ban logic. Saul interpreted command “in his own way”; war “after fashion of other wars” = profanation of the holy (Hertzberg via Tsumura).
- **Quote:** “This was in direct disobedience to the divine command in v. 3. The purpose of this war was not to gain spoil but to fulfill God’s ancient command. … ‘partial fulfillment is not a possibility’ in the logic of ban.”

### C-R5-19 | *nḥm* 15:11 — emotive/performative divine “regret”
- **Claim:** Word of Lord to Samuel: “I regret (*niḥamtî*) that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following me and has not carried out (*hēqîm*) my words.” *niḥamtî* performative perfect (also Gen 6:7); emotive + performative; anthropopathic yet “dynamic in his interaction with his creation.” *nḥm* key word: vv. 11, 35 and twice in 29 (“change mind”); also God moderating judgment (2 Sam 24:16). “Turned away from following me” stronger than 13:13 “foolish.” Samuel angry; cries to Lord all night — prophet feels divine pathos.
- **Quote:** “Yahweh’s ‘regret’ (or ‘repentance’) is anthropopathic; ‘yet it conveys an important truth about a God who is not impassive or static, but dynamic in his interaction with his creation.’”
- **Locus:** 15:10–11 / pp. 395–396 / slice ~L1521–1545
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[1-samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]]
- **Flag:** *nḥm* — controversy / theology

### C-R5-20 | Saul’s self-deception; sacrifice ≠ ban; “your God”
- **Claim:** Saul erects *yad* monument at Carmel (Judah), goes to Gilgal. Greets Samuel: “I have carried out the word of the Lord” — self-deception. Samuel’s poetic question about bleating/lowing cattle. Saul’s excuses: impersonal passive “they have been brought”; “the people spared”; best “to sacrifice to the Lord, **your** God”; “we” destroyed the rest. Sacrifice ≠ ban: ban is total destruction as Yahweh’s share; sacrifice shares portions with men; God did not ask cultic sacrifice. Pronoun “your God” lightens Saul’s responsibility as people’s representative.
- **Quote:** “However, sacrifice and the ‘ban’ are not the same thing; the ‘ban’ is the total destruction, devoting everything to Yahweh as his share, while sacrifice usually provides portions for men. God had not asked for a cultic sacrifice.”
- **Locus:** 15:12–16 / pp. 396–399 / slice ~L1546–1618
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[herem]], [[1-samuel]]
- **Flag:** *ḥerem*

### C-R5-21 | Obedience better than sacrifice (15:22–23); reject word → rejected as king
- **Claim:** Central poetic prose: Lord delights in obeying voice more than burnt offerings/sacrifices; “obedience is better than sacrifice; attentiveness than the fat of rams.” Rebellion = sin of divination; presumption = wickedness and idolatry (*terāpîm*). Because Saul rejected word of Lord, Lord rejected him from being king — opposite of anointing (v. 17). Prophets attack sacrificial abuses not system as such (Isa, Jer, Hos, Amos, Mic; cf. 1 Sam 2:29). No ceremonial substitutes for rebellious self-will. Ch. 13 denied dynastic continuance; here Saul himself rejected; ch. 15 less excused (greed/presumption vs extreme threat). May foreshadow Endor (divination Saul later uses though he wiped it out).
- **Quote:** “Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice; attentiveness than the fat of rams!” / “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, he has rejected you from being king!”
- **Locus:** 15:17–23 / pp. 399–403 / slice ~L1620–1816
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[herem]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R5-22 | First confession (15:24–26): feared the people; democracy vs theocracy
- **Claim:** Saul: “I have sinned… transgressed the command of the Lord and your words, because I feared the people and listened to their voice.” Shift from claiming obedience to admitting disobedience via people-obedience — but still fails to grasp seriousness. *ḥāṭā’tî* performative perfect (“I am a sinner”). Asks “take my sin away” and return to worship; Samuel refuses: rejected word → rejected from being king. “In the biblical principle, democracy contradicts theocracy.” Not two contradictory endings (McCarter): persistence of Saul + Samuel’s concern + transition between confessions.
- **Quote:** “Saul listened to their voice instead of listening to God’s voice! … In the biblical principle, democracy contradicts theocracy.”

### C-R5-23 | Robe tear; kingdom to “neighbor”; *nḥm* dual sense (15:29 vs 11/35)
- **Claim:** Saul seizes hem of Samuel’s robe (ANE supplication gesture); tear = unintentional acted parable: Lord has torn kingdom of Israel from Saul **today** (legal perfect; realization future) and given it to **neighbor** better than you (= David; not Jonathan). **15:29:** “the Splendor of Israel (*nēṣaḥ yiśrā’ēl*) does not deceive and does not change his mind (*nḥm*), for he is not a man that he should change his mind.” Against McCarter gloss theory: no contradiction if **context/speaker** decide sense — in v. 29 (future decision) *nḥm* = “change one’s mind” **relationally**, paired with “deceive”; in vv. 11 and 35 same root = **emotive** “regret.” Tension remains as theological problem (why God lets things go wrong) but divine “repentance” ≠ human untruthfulness (// Num 23:19 motif).
- **Quote:** “while *nḥm* (Ni.) certainly means ‘to change one’s mind’ in the present context, the same verb in vv. 11 and 35 refers to God’s ‘regret.’ While in the former the word is paired with the term ‘to deceive’ and is used relationally, in the latter it functions emotively, expressing God’s inner feeling.”
- **Locus:** 15:27–29 / pp. 405–407 / slice ~L1849–1895

### C-R5-24 | Second confession (15:30): honor before elders / reputation
- **Claim:** Second “I have sinned!” but main concern is reputation: “please **honor me** before the elders of my people and before Israel” then return and worship “the Lord **your** God.” Unwilling to lose face; correct religious language without reality; contrast Psalm 51 / David. Pronouns **my people** / **your God** show Saul forgot Israel is Yahweh’s people and king is representative under God’s word (12:25), not owner. Samuel returns after Saul (personal concern or national order if rejection known); Saul worships **without** recovering relationship with God.
- **Quote:** “That his main concern is not with his sin can be seen from the following words: But now, please honor me before the elders of my people … . Instead of honoring God, Saul is concerned with honoring himself. He was unwilling to lose face before the people.”

### C-R5-26 | Samuel executes Agag: *ḥerem* completion, not sacrifice
- **Claim:** Dischronologized episode: still at Gilgal, Samuel has Agag brought. Agag comes *ma‘ădannōt* (“cheerfully”?); “Surely the bitterness of death is past!” Samuel’s poetic sentence: as Agag’s sword made women childless, so his mother childless among women. **Hews Agag to pieces before the Lord at Gilgal.** McCarter: LXX + “before the Lord” suggest sacrificial butchering / covenant-breaker symbolism. **Tsumura follows Hertzberg:** action takes event **from sphere of sacrifice into that of the ban**; // Achan (Josh 7). Samuel completes the *ḥerem* Saul neglected, devoting Agag to the Lord. C. H. Gordon: obligatory slaying of captured enemy heroes (// Iliad 6:55–60).
- **Quote:** “However, as Hertzberg holds, Samuel’s action rather ‘takes the event from the sphere of sacrifice into that of the ban’; see the punishment of Achan in Joshua 7. Instead of Saul, Samuel completed the performance of the ‘ban’ on the Amalekites, devoting Agag their king to the Lord.”
- **Locus:** 15:32–33 / pp. 408–411 / slice ~L1907–1950
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[herem]], [[amalekites]], [[saul]], [[1-samuel]]
- **Flag:** *ḥerem* / Agag execution

### C-R5-27 | Samuel–Saul break; final *nḥm*; inclusio with 15:1
- **Claim:** Samuel to Ramah, Saul to Gibeah of Saul (&lt;10 miles). 15:35: Samuel did not “see” (meet) Saul again until day of death; grieved over Saul — true pastor; link to 16:1. Lord **regretted** (*nḥm*) making Saul king over Israel (= v. 11 sense). Inclusio with 15:1 (“anoint you as a king over his people Israel”). Looks forward to appointment of one “better than” Saul (v. 28). Church/state symbolism secondary; clear OT ideology: king must listen to word of God the Divine King. Why Saul rejected / David not condemned to death after adultery-murder: both “righteousness” and “love and mercy” (→ Christ) — deferred to Introduction IX, C.
- **Quote:** “As for the Lord, he regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.” / “The phrase he had made Saul king over Israel corresponds to the initial statement of Samuel … thus forming an inclusio.”
- **Locus:** 15:34–35 / pp. 411 / slice ~L1952–1967
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-samuel]]
- **Flag:** *nḥm*

### C-R5-28 | Ahijah/Eli link; Eli house // Saul house
- **Claim:** Priest Ahijah (son of Ahitub, brother of Ichabod, Phinehas–Eli line) wears/carries ephod with Saul — oracular support for war. Gordon: v. 3 links failed house of Eli with failed house of Saul (one man left, 2:33). Background for interrupted inquiry 14:18–19 and lots 14:41–42.
- **Quote:** “R. P. Gordon notes that v. 3 links the failed house of Eli with the failed house of Saul, whose house also will be destroyed with just one man left; see 2:33.”
- **Locus:** 14:2–3 / pp. 357–359 / slice ~L690–740
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]]
